wine.name: Hamilton Russell Vineyards Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from the estate's own vines.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, close to the cold Atlantic at Hermanus, on stony, clay rich, low vigour soils derived from Bokkeveld shale.
wine.making: Made only from the estate's own Pinot Noir, the wine goes through its malolactic conversion in full and is aged about ten months in 228 litre barrels of tight grained French oak, a quarter to a third of them new in the house's sheets, before bottling at the estate.
wine.glass: Dark cherry and raspberry over forest floor and a savoury, earthy note that can make it seem backward in youth; juicy acidity and fine grained tannin, more structure and savour than sweetness of fruit.
wine.ageing: Often closed and earthy for its first few years, it opens with five or more in bottle and keeps well beyond a decade in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate's own name, kept for its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay alone.
The Wine of Origin ward nearest the sea of the three that bear the Hemel-en-Aarde name.
The Cape's certification of where the grapes were grown, here the ward named beside it.

records.table: Hamilton Russell Vineyards Pinot Noir comes from stony, clay rich shale in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley behind Hermanus, close to the cold sea. It is savoury and fine grained rather than sweet, so give a young bottle air and a cool pour.
records.story: In 1975 the chairman of one of South Africa's leading advertising companies bought a run down, undeveloped property in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley behind Hermanus, a place then almost unknown for wine. Vines went in from 1976, and in the same year the valley's first modern cellar was built on the farm. The first vintage came in 1981, a crop of many varieties; that year's Pinot Noir, from vines only four years old, was labelled Grand Vin Noir, and the first Chardonnay followed in 1982. In 1991 the founder's son took over and set the estate on two grapes alone, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and by 1994 he had completed the purchase of the estate and mapped its soils, keeping the vines on the stony, clay rich shale that suits them. The family later made wines of other grapes under other names, so the house's own name stays on those two. The valley it pioneered became a Wine of Origin ward in its own right, and Bouchard Finlayson, whose founding winemaker had made the early wines here, and Newton Johnson followed it into the Hemel-en-Aarde. The Pinot Noir is the measure of the Cape's cool south coast: the wine that showed, in the 1980s, that South Africa could grow Pinot Noir of savoury depth beside the sea.

wine.name: Galpin Peak Pinot Noir
wine.sites: The estate's Pinot Noir vineyards beneath Galpin Peak in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, densely planted on ancient, stony, clay rich Bokkeveld shale, shallow soils that keep the vines' vigour low.
wine.making: Aged about eleven months in French oak barrels, under a third of them new by the house's sheets, then given a few months more of élevage before bottling. In the strongest years chosen barrels are set aside as the Tête de Cuvée.
wine.glass: Plum, raspberry and mulberry with clove, nutmeg and a touch of violet, turning smoky and savoury as it matures; generous in structure, with fine tannin and a long, firm finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of the vintage, it gains savour for a decade and more, and the house's own sheets give it at least eight years.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The fynbos covered mountain above the vineyards, which gives the Pinot Noir its name.
The Wine of Origin ward of the lower valley behind Hermanus.
A barrel selection of Galpin Peak, bottled apart only in the strongest vintages.

records.table: Galpin Peak is Bouchard Finlayson's Pinot Noir, named for the mountain above its vineyards in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, a house founded with a Burgundian partner in 1989. Grown on stony shale and clay, it tastes of plum, raspberry and clove, firm and fine.
records.story: Bouchard Finlayson was set up in 1989 as a partnership between a Burgundian winemaker of the Bouchard family and a Cape winemaker who had made the early wines at Hamilton Russell next door, where in 1976 he had built the valley's first modern winery. The two set out to make Pinot Noir in the Burgundian manner, and the first vines on the new estate went in from 1989, by the house's own account. The first grapes, bought in, were crushed in February 1991 by one account, and the estate's own fruit followed. The Pinot Noir took the name of Galpin Peak, the fynbos covered mountain of about 810 metres that, with the Tower of Babel, shelters the valley from the north. In 2000 the estate was bought by a family of hoteliers, and the Cape winemaker stayed on as cellar master, later handing the making of the wine to a successor. From chosen barrels of the strongest years the house bottles a Tête de Cuvée apart, while a red blend of Italian grapes, Hannibal, shows the partners' wider curiosity. Galpin Peak is the house's answer to Burgundy on Cape shale: Pinot Noir from dense plantings on shallow, stony clay beneath a mountain, made to last.

wine.name: Family Vineyards Pinot Noir
wine.appellation: Wine of Origin Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from the family's own vineyards.
wine.sites: Several of the family's own parcels in the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, about nine kilometres from the Atlantic, the Mrs M vineyard among them, on decomposed granite over iron rich clay.
wine.making: Each parcel is fermented apart, a share of it as whole bunches that varies from site to site and year to year. The wine is aged about eleven months in 228 litre barrels made in Burgundy, under a third of them new, then spends a further five months in stainless steel before bottling.
wine.glass: Rose petal and musk over red cherry and wild strawberry, with a faint note of fynbos; fresh, lively acidity and fine tannin, perfumed and light on its feet rather than heavy.
wine.ageing: Charming within a few years of the vintage, it keeps its perfume and gains savour for eight to ten years from a good vintage.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: Made only from the parcels the family farms itself, blended together.
The Wine of Origin ward of the higher valley, inland of the lower valley ward.

records.table: Newton Johnson's Family Vineyards Pinot Noir blends the family's own parcels on decomposed granite in the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, close to the Atlantic. It smells of rose, musk and red cherry and stays fresh and fine, so serve it cool.
records.story: Newton Johnson joins two family names. In 1995, by the family's own account, a Cape Wine Master and his wife, born a Newton, moved to the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley and built a cellar before they planted any vines; the Newton side, the house says, traces its roots to Falkirk in Scotland. The first vintage, in 1997, was made from bought in fruit. The family planted its first Pinot Noir on its own farm in 2003, on decomposed granite over clay about nine kilometres from the sea, and the founders' sons came to lead the house in the cellar and the vines. As those vineyards matured, the family drew its Pinot Noir more and more from its own slopes. The Family Vineyards Pinot Noir is the blend of those parcels, made entirely from estate fruit, while single blocks, Windansea and Seadragon among them, are bottled on their own. The house also makes wines of other grapes, Albariño among them, but Pinot Noir is the grape it is known by. The Family Vineyards bottling makes the case for the upper valley: higher and more granitic than the valley below, it gives Pinot Noir of perfume and lift rather than weight.

wine.name: Art of Chardonnay
wine.sites: One pocket of a single vineyard on a southern slope of the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, where seams of quartz run through clay loam over Bokkeveld shale.
wine.making: Only the free run juice is fermented, in French oak barrels with about a third new, most of it with wild yeast. The wine then rests on its lees for ten to eleven months through a full malolactic conversion, without stirring, and after a barrel selection it is bottled unfined and unfiltered.
wine.glass: Ripe lemon, lemon curd and a struck match note, with hazelnut and a gentle touch of cardamom; taut acidity carried on a creamy texture from the lees, and a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Tight on release, it opens after three or four years and keeps for a decade from a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though air helps a young bottle; a wide white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's barrel selected Chardonnay from one pocket of a single vineyard, at the head of its range.
The Wine of Origin ward on the ridge at the top of the Hemel-en-Aarde.

records.table: Art of Chardonnay is Creation's barrel selected Chardonnay from one pocket of quartz and clay on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, a house founded on unplanted land in 2002. Expect lemon curd, struck match and hazelnut over taut acidity; pour it cool, not cold.
records.story: Creation was founded in 2002 by a Swiss winemaker and his South African born wife, who bought land on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge that had never been planted to vines. The first Pinot Noir went in during 2003, from virus free material by the house's account, and in the same year the estate planted Grenache, by one account the first in the Hemel-en-Aarde. The cellar was finished and the first harvest brought in by 2006, and within about five years the bare slopes had become a working wine farm. The Ridge is one of three wards that carry the Hemel-en-Aarde name, and its soils mix stony clay and Bokkeveld shale with seams of quartz. The house came to sort its Chardonnay into tiers, from Glenn's to the Reserve, and at the head it set the Art of Chardonnay, drawn from one pocket of a single vineyard where quartz runs through the clay, chosen barrel by barrel and bottled in numbered bottles. Beside it stands the Art of Pinot Noir from the same ridge. The wine is the youngest of the valley's Chardonnay stories, and its case is that a ridge planted only this century can give Chardonnay of tension and texture to set beside the older houses lower down.

wine.name: Hope Marguerite Chenin Blanc
wine.grapes: Chenin Blanc alone, from old vines.
wine.sites: The farm's two oldest Chenin Blanc blocks at Bot River, planted in 1974 and 1978.
wine.making: Fermented with its own wild yeasts in 400 litre French oak barrels, a small share of them new, and left on its gross lees for ten to eleven months with regular stirring before bottling.
wine.glass: Pear, white peach and lemon with honeysuckle and a flinty, struck note; a lean, taut palate with a gentle sweetness from the oak and a saline finish.
wine.ageing: Taut on release, it gains honey and breadth over five to ten years from a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a wide white wine glass.

label.means: The name of a woman of the family, given to the house's barrel fermented old vine Chenin Blanc.
The Wine of Origin ward at the western gateway to Walker Bay, cooled by its lagoon.

records.table: Hope Marguerite is Beaumont's barrel fermented Chenin Blanc from the farm's oldest blocks at Bot River, planted in 1974 and 1978. It tastes of pear, white peach and honeysuckle with a flinty edge, lean and saline, so pour it cool beside fish.
records.story: The farm at Bot River, Compagnes Drift, began in the 1700s as an outpost of the Dutch East India Company, a supply farm for fruit, vegetables, dairy, wine and flour, and by the family's account it keeps one of the oldest working watermills in South Africa. In 1974 the Beaumont family bought it, derelict, and set about replanting the vineyards; the two Chenin Blanc blocks that make Hope Marguerite date from 1974 and 1978. For years the farm's grapes went to the co-operative, until in 1994 the family left the co-operative system and began to bottle under the Beaumont name. The first Hope Marguerite followed with the 1997 vintage, by the house's account: a barrel fermented Chenin Blanc named for a woman of the family, the founding husband's mother as most accounts tell it. The house also claims the first single varietal Mourvèdre bottled in South Africa. In 2015 the founders' son and his wife took over the running of the farm. Hope Marguerite shows what old Chenin Blanc can do in Bot River, the ward the Wines of South Africa body calls the gateway to Walker Bay, cooled by its lagoon and the bay. It is a reminder that the district is more than Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
